title: Chapter XXXIV

teacherSummary.text: Darcy unexpectedly proposes, insulting her family and confessing he loves her against his will. Elizabeth rejects him angrily, accusing him of ruining Jane's happiness and wronging Wickham, and calling him ungentlemanly.

vocabulary.definition: To move with a violent, irregular action
vocabulary.context: She continued in very agitating reflections till the sound of Lady Catherine’s carriage made her feel how unequal she was to encounter Charlotte’s observation, and hurried her away to her room.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “agitate”: -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To carry from one place to another
vocabulary.context: Elizabeth noticed every sentence conveying the idea of uneasiness, with an attention which it had hardly received on the first perusal.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “convey”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: The act of carefully viewing or examining
vocabulary.context: Elizabeth noticed every sentence conveying the idea of uneasiness, with an attention which it had hardly received on the first perusal.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “perusal”: per- (Latin per, "through, thoroughly"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: My feelings will not be repressed.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “repress”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: He spoke well, but there were feelings besides those of the heart to be detailed, and he was not more eloquent on the subject of tenderness than of pride.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “detail”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To give, cause, or produce by striking, or as if by striking
vocabulary.context: Darcy’s shameful boast of what misery he had been able to inflict, gave her a keener sense of her sister’s sufferings.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “inflict”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To look down upon from a place that is over or above
vocabulary.context: But perhaps,” added he, stopping in his walk, and turning towards her, “these offences might have been overlooked, had not your pride been hurt by my honest confession of the scruples that had long prevented my forming any serious design.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “overlook”: over- (Old English ofer, "over"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: That which stands in the way, or opposes
vocabulary.context: His sense of her inferiority—of its being a degradation—of the family obstacles which judgment had always opposed to inclination, were dwelt on with a warmth which seemed due to the consequence he was wounding, but was very unlikely to recommend his suit.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “obstacle”: ob- (Latin ob, "against, toward"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The act of reducing in rank, character, or reputation, or of abasing
vocabulary.context: His sense of her inferiority—of its being a degradation—of the family obstacles which judgment had always opposed to inclination, were dwelt on with a warmth which seemed due to the consequence he was wounding, but was very unlikely to recommend his suit.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “degradation”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + -ation (Latin -atio, "the act or result of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: An interruption of a state of peace or quiet
vocabulary.context: His complexion became pale with anger, and the disturbance of his mind was visible in every feature.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “disturbance”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not") + urb (Latin urbs, "city") + -ance (Latin -antia, "state of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

context.history: A proposal from a man of Darcy's wealth was extraordinary for a woman of Elizabeth's means.

significance: The climax of the first half: pride and prejudice collide openly.
discussionQuestions: Which of Elizabeth's accusations is fair, and which is mistaken?
Where does conflict appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with class and social mobility?

items.prompt: How does Darcy describe his love?
What two charges does Elizabeth make?
options: Ruining Jane's happiness and wronging Wickham

items.prompt: What is ironic about the proposal?
options: Darcy expects acceptance but is rejected

items.prompt: In the line “She continued in very agitating reflections till the sound of Lady Catherine’s carriage made her feel how unequal she was to encounter Charlotte’s observation, and hurried her away to her room.”, what does “agitating” most nearly mean?

To carry from one place to another
The act of carefully viewing or examining

options: The act of carefully viewing or examining
To carry from one place to another
To move with a violent, irregular action

Darcy expects acceptance but is rejected

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXXIV,” how does Austen show the first proposal? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the conflict you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXXIV develops the idea of the first proposal. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of conflict and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses conflict in Chapter XXXIV to complicate the reader's understanding of the first proposal. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXXIV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the first proposal responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXXIV as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the first proposal. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: Elizabeth’s astonishment was beyond expression. She stared, coloured, doubted, and was silent. This he considered sufficient encouragement, and the avowal of all that he felt and had long felt for her, immediately followed. He spoke well, but there were feelings besides those of the heart to be detailed, and he was not more eloquent on the subject of tenderness than of pride. His sense of her inferiority—of its being a degradation—of the family obstacles which judgment had always opposed to inclination, were dwelt on with a warmth which seemed due to the consequence he was wounding, but was very unlikely to recommend his suit.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XXXIV”?
options: The wedding night and its catastrophe

annotationFocus.label: Characterization

annotationFocus.lookFor: gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Which of Elizabeth's accusations is fair, and which is mistaken? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are agitating, conveying, perusal, repressed, detailed. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “She continued in very agitating reflections till the sound of Lady Catherine’s carriage made her feel how unequal she was to encounter Charlotte’s observation, and hurried her away to her room.” Webster's says: To move with a violent, irregular action. Now the word history: “agitate”: -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “convey”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “perusal”: per- (Latin per, "through, thoroughly"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. A proposal from a man of Darcy's wealth was extraordinary for a woman of Elizabeth's means. Why does this chapter matter? The climax of the first half: pride and prejudice collide openly. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for conflict.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see conflict, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to the first proposal.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Conflict, Characterization, Irony.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of conflict. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: Elizabeth’s astonishment was beyond expression. She stared, coloured, doubted, and was silent. This he considered sufficient encouragement, and the avowal of all that he felt and had long felt for her, immediately followed. He spoke well, but there were feelings besides those of the heart to be detailed, and he was not more eloquent on the subject of tenderness than of pride. His sense of her inferiority—of its being a degradation—of the family obstacles which judgment had always opposed to inclination, were dwelt on with a warmth which seemed due to the consequence he was wounding, but was very unlikely to recommend his suit.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Conflict, Characterization, Irony: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XXXIV,” how does Austen show the first proposal? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the conflict you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about the first proposal, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how conflict shapes the first proposal. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
